impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. Banks and entities that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis were time-barred from pursuing breach of contract and takings claims against the government.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity and finality for the government and regulated entities regarding the strict application of the § 2501 limitations period, reducing exposure to stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors relying on class action tolling to preserve government claims in the Court of Federal Claims will find that strategy unavailable, requiring them to file individual claims within the statutory deadline.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether copyright infringement damages against the government must be assessed by deferring to the terms of an existing license agreement, and whether the trial court's 'book of wisdom' approach and non-compensatory damages award were legally permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts are not compelled to defer to existing license agreement terms when calculating copyright infringement damages and may instead use a hypothetical negotiation approach. However, the court vacated part of the damages award, holding that the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and improperly assessed non-compensatory damages against the government.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders retain flexibility in proving damages through hypothetical negotiation rather than being bound to potentially below-market license rates established in prior agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains copyright holders from recovering damages that exceed actual compensatory harm, and the rejection of certain 'book of wisdom' evidence may limit the evidentiary tools available in government copyright infringement cases.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations for a Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) claim had expired before the plaintiff filed suit, given the plaintiff's knowledge of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a $11.5 million-plus jury verdict for trade secret misappropriation, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or had reason to know of the misappropriation more than three years before it brought suit, entitling EOFlow to judgment as a matter of law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides important protection for companies accused of trade secret misappropriation by strictly enforcing the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, preventing plaintiffs from strategically delaying suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must be highly vigilant about filing suit promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, or risk forfeiting their DTSA claims entirely.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating it. The court affirmed that Ford was liable for trade secret misappropriation of Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that software licensors can pursue trade secret misappropriation claims when licensees develop competing products using proprietary knowledge gained during the licensing relationship, and broadens admissible damages theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop replacement software after licensing proprietary technology face significant trade secret misappropriation exposure, even when the license relationship has ended.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not included in a prior IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to estop one ground and failure to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The court held that the evidence was inadequate to show that a skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have been expected to discover the prior art references at issue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent infringement cases retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court even after IPR proceedings, as courts must carefully evaluate the reasonableness of prior art searches before applying estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a higher burden in establishing IPR estoppel, potentially allowing accused infringers to raise invalidity arguments in district court that were not pursued in IPR.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent's claim to priority from a provisional application is defeated when the non-provisional application corrects an alleged typographical error in the provisional, and whether the intervening public disclosure of a compound (nirmatrelvir/Paxlovid) then anticipates the patent claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering coronavirus protease inhibitors, holding that the change from 'C2' to 'C1' in an alkyl substituent definition was not a correctable obvious typographical error. Because the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional application, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides certainty for generic and competing pharmaceutical manufacturers that intervening disclosures can invalidate patents that fail to maintain consistent priority chain support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies must exercise extreme care in drafting provisional applications, as even minor discrepancies (such as a single character difference) can break the priority chain and expose claims to anticipation by intervening art.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a single jury question covering infringement for multiple patents on a verdict form requires vacatur, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 eligibility analysis and jury instructions regarding the '495 patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's single question covering infringement across all asserted patents was deficient. The court also vacated the § 101 eligibility determination for the '495 patent for further Alice step two analysis, while affirming eligibility for the '887 and '371 patents related to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement of patent-specific verdict forms, preventing a single infringement finding from sweeping in multiple patents without differentiated analysis.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents must ensure verdict forms contain separate infringement questions for each patent, adding complexity and risk of inconsistent verdicts at trial.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case non-exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, finding the claims abstract. The court vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, signaling that pursuing clearly patent-ineligible claims may warrant fee-shifting under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defenses for agricultural technology companies accused of infringing data collection and processing patents, and increases the potential for fee recovery in cases involving clearly ineligible patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on data collection and processing methods in agriculture and other industries face heightened § 101 invalidity risk, and may face exceptional case fee-shifting if they pursue enforcement of such patents.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for two patents ('761 and '700) related to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications, finding further analysis needed under Alice. However, it affirmed eligibility for the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, upholding the jury verdict against LG for willful infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Standard-essential patent holders in digital communications can enforce patents covering specific non-uniform constellation implementations, and damages awards supported by proper expert testimony will be upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards may face significant patent infringement liability, including willfulness findings, and § 101 eligibility challenges may be insufficient to avoid trial.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in the weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta, upholding the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the district court must require a bond pending appeal to protect the enjoined party from potential wrongful injunction damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies can obtain preliminary injunctions to block generic entry before patent expiration, preserving market exclusivity during litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies are blocked from market entry, but the requirement of a bond pending appeal provides some financial protection against wrongful injunctions. Branded companies must post meaningful bonds.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement has constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the exclusionary right to sue third parties for infringement maintains sufficient constitutional standing even after granting an exclusive license. The retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the exclusive licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure exclusive license agreements to retain enforcement rights while granting broad commercialization licenses, enabling continued enforcement against infringers without joining the licensee.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot easily defeat patent infringement suits by challenging the patent owner's standing based on the existence of an exclusive license, narrowing available procedural defenses.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' functions should be treated as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling regarding 'executable program code' limitations, finding that further analysis was warranted in light of the intervening Dyfan precedent on means-plus-function claim interpretation. The court remanded for new factual and legal submissions on whether § 112(f) applies. Separately, the court affirmed invalidity of a different patent claim under § 102 anticipation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders may avoid indefiniteness rulings where claim terms like 'executable program code configured to' are erroneously classified as means-plus-function terms, preserving enforceability of software-implemented claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the certainty of indefiniteness-based invalidity rulings for software claims, as courts must now more carefully analyze whether functional claim language triggers § 112(f).

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's remand determination that three government debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit to a foreign steel producer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and ordered reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that the debt-to-equity conversions conferred countervailable benefits. The court found that Commerce's original equityworthiness analysis was proper and should not have been overturned on remand, restoring countervailing duties on imported Korean steel products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from the reinstatement of countervailing duties that protect against subsidized foreign competition, preserving the integrity of trade remedy enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel producers and importers face reinstated countervailing duties, increasing costs and potentially limiting market access for subsidized products in the U.S. market.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence, particularly regarding dependent claims reciting a 'predetermined time delay' for reporting sensor information.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination for the challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved a third-party (Qualcomm) filing IPR petitions on the same day as the statutory deadline for the party actually sued for infringement (Roambee), raising concerns about potential circumvention of the IPR time bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in logistics and IoT technology gain protection against potentially deficient obviousness challenges, particularly where the PTAB's analysis of specific claim limitations was insufficient.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR filings to challenge competitor patents may face scrutiny regarding the timing and coordination of such petitions relative to the statutory time bar.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement complaint on the pleadings based on obviousness grounds from a prior IPR, and whether the resulting case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 warranting attorney fees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint where the PTAB had already invalidated most claims on the same obviousness grounds, but reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanction. The court held that the grounds presented were insufficient to support a finding that the case was exceptional or that counsel acted in bad faith.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects patent holders and their counsel from fee-shifting and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims on surviving patent claims, even when related claims were invalidated in IPR.
impacts.negativeImplications: Defendants may still face patent infringement suits on claims that survived IPR, though they can seek dismissal on the pleadings when the surviving claims are vulnerable to the same invalidity grounds.
